US consumer sentiment falls to five-month low in October
article:
(Oct 9): US consumer sentiment fell in early October and views of current economic conditions hit an all-time low as inflation weighed on households.

The University of Michigan’s preliminary sentiment index decreased to 46.3, the lowest reading since May, according to the survey released Friday. That was below the median estimate of 47.6 in a Bloomberg survey of economists.

The current conditions gauge sank to 44.7, the lowest on record, from 50.9 in the previous month. The expectations index rose to 47.3 from 46.3, the first increase since July.

Consumer sentiment continued to worsen as gasoline prices remained elevated, borrowing costs rose and hiring slowed.

Consumers expect prices to rise 4.7% over the next year, up slightly from 4.6% in the previous month. They also saw costs rising at an annual rate of 3.5% over the next five to 10 years, slightly more than what consumers estimated in September.

Higher fuel prices are weighing on consumers already frustrated with persistent inflation and the rising cost of living. In recent months, overall price increases have been outpacing pay gains, further pressuring household budgets.

See also: US 30-year yields return to 2002 high with crude back above US$100

Sentiment of lower-income consumers and those with smaller stock portfolios dropped steeply this month, Joanne Hsu, director of the survey, said in a statement. And increases in sentiment among Democrats and Republicans were offset by a decline among independents.

“Despite their differences, consumers of all political identifications agree that the outlook for the economy has softened since the beginning of the year prior to the Iran conflict," Hsu said.

While consumer sentiment has been historically weak much of this year, spending has remained healthy. A stable labour market and buoyant stock market are supporting outlays on a wide range of goods and services.

See also: US yields fall from 2002 high as oil dips, Bessent vows on debt

Consumers’ perception of their current financial situation held steady this month, though their view of buying conditions for durable goods fell to a record low due to concerns over higher interest rates.

The survey period includes responses from Sept 22 to Oct 5.

A special report on consumers' response to higher gasoline prices released Friday found only about 31% expect to spend as usual over the coming year. Just over half said they would cut back spending on items such as households goods, cars, dining out and vacations.

title: US stocks edge higher as oil slips, AI bubble fears recede
article:
(Oct 9): US stocks rose as oil prices fell and investor concerns about the artificial-intelligence (AI) spending spree eased.

The S&P 500 Index rose 0.2%, while the Nasdaq 100 advanced 0.2% as of 9.47am. A report that OpenAI expects to reach or exceed US$70 billion ($89.7 billion) in annualised revenue by year-end helped alleviate anxiety over the durability of the AI boom after an earlier report suggested the company’s sales would fall short of expectations. Others on Wall Street are pushing back on the narrative that the market is witnessing an AI bubble.

“People are worried, and that’s not a sign of a bubble,” Christian Mueller-Glissman, a Goldman Sachs strategist, said in an interview on Bloomberg Television. “Usually, when you’re in the bubble, there’s a lot of exuberance, and people have FOMO.”

He also pointed to the J-curve dynamic of technology investment, in which substantial upfront capital spending can take time to translate into revenue growth and productivity gains.

As the bull market in US stocks approaches its fourth anniversary, it’s showing few signs of stress with corporate profits rock-solid and the S&P 500 near a record. A 117% advance in the equities gauge since 2022 makes it the third-largest bull market of that length in data going back to 1947, according to CFRA.

When the rally extends to a fifth year, the historical average gain is 21%, CFRA data show. Theoretically, that leaves plenty of room for the rally to broaden out beyond technology megacaps that have driven the lion’s share of gains since October 2022.

See also: US stocks fall from all-time highs on inflation worry

Still, signs of strain are emerging across the AI-infrastructure trade. Nvidia Corp-backed Firmus Grid Ltd shelved plans for an Australian initial public offering just days after signalling strong demand for a deal that would have valued the data centre company at US$30 billion. Credit-default swap spreads on Oracle Corp reached new highs, as Morgan Stanley warned that project delays could weigh on the company’s debt.

Banks will kick off earnings season in earnest next week. The sector has underperformed the S&P 500 by 11% over the past month and investors will be looking for data and commentary regarding the state of the US consumer.

“The biggest signal we will get will not be from the consumer companies but the banks. It will be interesting to see how bank management characterises the consumer from spending to credit,” said Joe Gilbert, portfolio manager at Integrity Asset Management. “We will be looking to see if credit has taken a leg down or if the K-shaped economy starts to converge.”

See also: S&P 500 climbs to record high on earnings optimism

In corporate news, Delta Air Lines Inc cut its adjusted earnings per share forecast for the full year and shares dropped. Apple Inc shares fell 2.5% on a report that the company cut component orders for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max amid weaker-than-expected demand. SpaceX shares are higher after Elon Musk’s rocket and AI company said it acquired low-band spectrum that will enable it to use its Starlink satellites to become a “major mobile carrier” in the US.
• Shares in optical-equipment makers rally after Lumentum notes that its components are “completely sold out” through early 2029 on demand from tech companies clamouring for faster AI data centres.
• Travel stocks are in focus today after high fuel costs forced Delta Air Lines to reduce its full-year outlook. The parent company for Vans and The North Face is rising after receiving an upgrade.
• Watch health insurers after Humana Inc shares surged on the company’s improved performance on crucial Medicare Advantage quality ratings. Shares of CVS Health Corp underperformed as ratings for some of its largest plans deteriorated.
• Shares in tower companies gained on SpaceX’s plan to acquire a nationwide low-band spectrum licence portfolio, a deal analysts said is a positive catalyst for the sector.

title: Tesla drops ‘self-driving’ branding to appease Europe regulators
article:
(Oct 9): Tesla Inc is backing away from its full self-driving branding to help secure approval for the driver-assistance system in Europe, distancing the company from a name that has drawn criticism as dangerously misleading.

The automaker has begun using the name “Tesla Assisted Driving” on its European websites in recent days. The US version of the same site is continuing to use “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” for the technology.

Tesla’s driver-assistance branding has long been a point of contention with regulators, safety advocates and even some Tesla customers, who say the name gives the impression of full autonomy even though drivers must still be alert and ready to take control of their vehicles. Chief executive officer Elon Musk has also been faulted by critics for pushing overly aggressive or unfounded claims about Tesla vehicles’ capabilities.

The California Department of Motor Vehicles last year threatened to suspend Tesla’s sales in the state over allegedly misleading marketing of driver-assistance technology. Authorities backed down after the company took “corrective action,” including phasing out its Autopilot branding and specifying when Full Self-Driving — also known as FSD — must have driver supervision.

FSD is a significant financial driver for Tesla’s automotive business, which typically charges drivers US$99 a month for the system. It’s also key to Musk’s efforts to refashion the carmaker as a tech-forward company pioneering autonomous vehicles and robotics.

Tesla is now seeking to bring the FSD system to Europe, which has been slow to embrace the technology. When Dutch regulators in April approved FSD, they emphasised that it was a more restrictive version than what is used in the US and said in a statement that “a vehicle with FSD Supervised is not self-driving”.

See also: Singapore to trial point-to-point driverless rides across Punggol

The company continues to seek approval in other countries across the continent.
